notes: kind='essay' means the winner published the essay text (full or substantial excerpts). kind='breakdown' means the winner published a detailed account of what they wrote and how, but not the essay text itself. No essay text is reproduced here; all analysis is original paraphrase. At most one short quote per item.

items: Leadership and influence: concrete examples of driving change, solving problems or delivering projects with visible results
Networking: building professional relationships that produce real outcomes and bring people together
Course choice: how the selected UK courses equip you to tackle a pressing challenge (growth, climate resilience, security, sustainable development)
Career plan: a realistic short-, medium- and long-term roadmap showing commitment to positive change and ties with the UK
Applicants must write their own answers; AI-generated or plagiarised answers are prohibited and screened for
Academic merit
Quality of the study plan / proposal
Potential impact on the development of the home country
Applicants are told to link each answer explicitly to these criteria (detailed scoring sheet: https://cscuk.fcdo.gov.uk/selection-criteria-for-assessment-of-applications/)
Quality and feasibility of the proposal / statement of grant purpose, and fit with the host country and award
Qualifications: academic and professional record, relevant training, achievements, activities and language preparation
Contribution to the Fulbright mission: advancing knowledge and mutual understanding between nations
Practical factors: host-country capacity to supervise/affiliate, cohort diversity
Nomination by the sending partner (home ministry/agency) based on its own ranking of applicants
Admission by the Hungarian university, including entrance exam/interview (a minimum score is required to be considered)
Motivation letter and documents assessed by the university for fit with the chosen programme
Note: the public Apply page gives procedure, not a scoring rubric; the per-year Call for Applications PDFs hold the detail
Embassy-led first screening on documents, including the field of study and research programme plan
Written exams and interview run by the Japanese embassy/consulate
Placement preference and acceptance by a Japanese university supervisor
Recommendation letter and academic record; detailed criteria are in the yearly Application Guidelines
Academic ability meeting the university's admission bar
Evidence of significant barriers faced (social, financial, personal, practical, health)
Track record of leadership and service in the community
Commitment to giving back to Africa (at Edinburgh, specifically to climate action)
Age and residency rules; women, refugees and people with disabilities are encouraged
Outstanding intellectual ability / academic excellence
Reasons for choice of course: why this Cambridge degree, and readiness for it
Commitment to improving the lives of others (past, present and planned)
Capacity for leadership and how it will have impact
Literary and scholastic attainment: intellectual curiosity and academic excellence
Energy to use one's talents to the full, shown in sustained activities outside class
Moral character: truth, courage, devotion to duty, care for the weak, fellowship
Moral force of character and instincts to lead, with interest in others
Same four criteria apply in every constituency (West Africa, Kenya, etc.)
Leadership ability
Exemplary character and integrity
Academic aptitude and intellectual ability
Empathy and intercultural competency
Open-mindedness
Entrepreneurial spirit and ability to read and act on change
Candidate's track record of academic excellence
Reputation and international policy of the nominating French institution
Fit with French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs cooperation priorities
Assessed by subject panels; candidates are nominated by a French institution, not self-nominated
Scholarships go to 'outstanding' students; each joint-master consortium sets and runs its own selection
Typical consortium criteria (check each programme site): academic record, motivation letter, relevance of experience, language skills, references
Demonstrated leadership experience (in work and civic life)
Relevant work experience
Clear plan for how the studies will contribute to sustainable development in the home country
Motivation letter and experience forms must be consistent with the CV
Note: page returned 403 to the checker on 2026-10-07; criteria paraphrased from SI's published programme description
Multi-stage selection: embassy or university first round, NIIED second round, university admission
Personal statement and study plan judged for motivation, clarity of goals and fit with Korea
Academic record (minimum CGPA) and recommendation letters
Note: NIIED site timed out for the checker; criteria paraphrased from the GKS application guidelines
Merit: quality of degrees, transcripts and professional qualifications
Viability and relevance of the study/research plan to the oil and gas industry
Link between previous study, proposed course and the sector
MSc statement of purpose capped at 500 words; PhD proposal capped at 5 pages
Professional membership; publications (PhD)
No single funder; for general graduate statements, map your text to the target programme's stated criteria
Common core: academic preparation, clear purpose, fit with programme, evidence of impact

items.title: Chevening essays of an Uzbek master's scholar (Leadership and Influence)
items.author: Jo'shqinbek Ismailov

criteria.how: Shows fast promotion on a renewable-energy project (analyst to commercial director within months) and being pulled onto projects in two neighbouring countries.
Second example: he trained colleagues in financial management over two years, which multiplied the team's capacity.

structure.what: Opens with his view that good leaders combine teamwork with personal excellence.
Career jump on an energy project, with timeframes to prove pace.
Coaching three colleagues so he could move to higher-level analysis.
Says UK study will sharpen leadership at national and international level.

techniques: Short time markers (three months, six months) make progress feel concrete
Two contrasting examples: own advancement vs growing other people
Ends by tying leadership growth to the degree
weaknesses: Results are mostly titles and promotions; few outcome numbers (money saved, MW delivered, people served)
Opening principle is generic and could belong to anyone
borrow: Pair one 'I delivered' story with one 'I built others' story
Use timestamps to show trajectory without bragging
Close by naming the leadership skill the degree will upgrade
items.exercise: Write two 120-word paragraphs: one where you led a result, one where you made someone else more capable. Give each a date range and one number.

items.title: Chevening essays of an Uzbek master's scholar (Networking)
items.author: Jo'shqinbek Ismailov

criteria.how: A presentation at a UN agriculture workshop in Rome led senior officials to consult him later in Tashkent: a contact turned into a working relationship.
Volunteered to collect feasibility data for an energy firm, which then treated him as an expert.

structure.what: Networking needs patience and ethics.
Nine years of international exposure.
International event leads to an ongoing advisory link.
Giving value first builds a trusted relationship.
Plans to link with UK energy specialists and the Chevening alumni body.

techniques: Shows a relationship's 'after' (they came back to him) rather than just meeting people
Names a UN forum for credibility
Explains the mechanism (transparency) behind his networking
Ends with a specific UK target community
weaknesses: Outcome of the relationships stays qualitative; no project or policy that resulted
Opening metaphor is decorative and spends words
borrow: Prove a contact became a relationship by showing the follow-up
Name what you gave first, not only what you got
Name the exact UK community you will join
items.exercise: Pick one professional relationship. In 150 words describe how it started, what you offered first, and what it produced six months later.

items.title: Chevening essays of an Uzbek master's scholar (Studying in the UK)
items.author: Jo'shqinbek Ismailov

criteria.how: Starts from his own gap (fieldwork without systems theory) and his country's slow uptake of modern energy methods.
Three energy master's programmes (Durham, Sussex, Dundee) each matched to a distinct need: socio-technical balance, low-carbon policy, practical economics/internships.

structure.what: Names the knowledge he lacks.
Why that gap matters for his country.
One paragraph per course with one distinctive reason each.
From national specialist to regional expert.

techniques: Different reason for each course instead of repeating 'world-class'
Cites rankings sparingly as supporting evidence
Personal skills gap as the hook
weaknesses: Leans on league-table positions, which the committee already knows
Few named modules or academics, so fit feels generic
borrow: Start with the skill you lack, not with praise for the UK
Give every course its own unique justification
Name one module or research centre per course
items.exercise: List your three courses. For each, write one sentence naming a module and the exact problem from your job it will help you solve.

items.title: Chevening essays of an Uzbek master's scholar (Career Plan)
items.author: Jo'shqinbek Ismailov
items.quote: Neighborhood is traditional culture in Uzbekistan; neighbors are closer than relatives are.

criteria.how: Short term: government role in named state energy companies; medium term: management plus international consulting; long term: an independent renewable-energy research institute.

criteria.c: Commitment to tackle a pressing issue
criteria.how: Argues his country needs home-grown experts, using a case where foreign-drafted rules ignored local custom of selling power between neighbours.

structure.what: Three horizons with year ranges.
Over-reliance on outside consultants.
A 2015 regulation that clashed with local practice.
Positions himself as the bridge between global practice and local culture.
Chevening as an investment in that bridge.

techniques: Named target employers make short-term goals checkable
A cultural detail turns a policy point into a memorable story
Positions himself as a translator between systems
weaknesses: Long-term institute lacks funding or partner detail
Few measurable targets (capacity, policies, people trained)
borrow: Use one local, cultural example to show why outsiders fail
Name the organisation for your first post-study role
Give each horizon a year range and a deliverable
items.exercise: Write a 3-line career table (0-2 yrs, 3-5 yrs, 10 yrs): role, organisation, one measurable deliverable. Then add a 60-word local story that proves why you, not an outsider, must do it.

items.title: My Chevening Journey, Part 1: Leadership Essay
items.author: Samuel Wairimu
items.quote: I will broaden my knowledge, competencies and networks

criteria.how: Founded a mentorship programme in 2014 after spotting falling motivation among pupils; it grew from five mentors to fifty schools and later funded bright needy students.
The work led to his appointment to a secondary-school board in 2015.

structure.what: States his leadership pattern: spot a need, assemble a team, deliver.
Situation, task, action and result in one paragraph.
Uses his own story of fees struggles and losing parents to motivate pupils.
Board appointment as proof.
How the scholarship scales his impact on poverty and inequality.

techniques: Personal adversity used as a tool in the story, not a plea
weaknesses: Only one example is published; reader cannot see how the others vary
Result focuses on scale, less on learner outcomes (grades, transitions)
borrow: Open with your leadership 'pattern' in one sentence, then prove it
Show scale with a before/after count
Mention a formal appointment that followed your work
items.exercise: Draft one STAR paragraph (max 180 words) about something you started. Include a starting number, an end number and one form of recognition.

items.title: My Chevening Journey, Part 2: Networking Essay tips
items.author: Samuel Wairimu

criteria.how: Used a banking contact to bring a microfinance CEO to train women; over 100 became clients and the lender opened in the area.
Coordinated a campaign team to very high turnout; a senior official then recruited him to a youth leadership role.

structure.what: Connect two parties to solve a community need.
Teamwork noticed by senior people, leading to a new role.
Plans with the Kenyan Chevening alumni on poverty and jobs.

techniques: Shows himself as the broker between groups
Each story ends with a lasting consequence
Ties networking to future alumni collaboration
weaknesses: The political-campaign example may read as partisan for a diplomatic programme
Little reflection on how he maintains relationships over time
borrow: Tell a story where you introduced two people and a result followed
End each example with what the relationship produced later
Name the alumni chapter you will work with
items.exercise: Recall a time you connected two people or groups. Write 120 words: who, why, what happened within a year, and one number.

items.title: My Chevening Journey, Part 3: Studying in the UK Essay
items.author: Samuel Wairimu

criteria.how: Frames poverty and inequality in Kenya despite investment as the reason for development study.
First choice is matched to an agriculture-and-development pathway and a named module and lecturer at Reading; Manchester and Edinburgh get distinct reasons (fieldwork, research placement).

structure.what: National paradox: investment without shared prosperity.
Pathway, named module and named lecturer.
Subject ranking plus field-trip element.
Historical approach and overseas research project.
Link to Kenya's national Vision 2030.

techniques: Names a module and the academic who teaches it
Each university gets a different practical feature
Anchors to a national development plan
weaknesses: The closing paragraph is brief and generic
He later changed choices, a reminder that course research should be finished before writing
borrow: Name one module and one academic for your top choice
Link your course to a named national plan
Give each choice a different hands-on feature
items.exercise: For your top course, find one module and the lecturer. Write 80 words on how that module changes one decision you make at work.

items.title: My Chevening Journey, Part 4: Career Essay Plan
items.author: Samuel Wairimu
items.quote: over 70% of Kenya's poor and hunger-stricken people live in rural areas

criteria.how: Short term: a community organisation turning smallholder farms into businesses with county and lender partners; medium term: county agriculture executive; long term: MP chairing an agriculture committee.

criteria.c: Commitment to change and UK links
criteria.how: Mentions working with UK firms' supply chains and the UK's development programmes in Kenya on food security.

structure.what: Rural concentration of poverty, cited to a named source.
Grassroots organisation with named partners.
Public office with a list of concrete services to fix.
National legislative role with policy and trade goals.
UK networks and alignment with UK aid priorities.

techniques: Sourced statistic in the first line
weaknesses: Electoral goals are hard to guarantee; could add a non-elected fallback
Few numerical targets for each stage
borrow: Open with one sourced statistic about your problem
Make each stage a bigger stage of the same mission
Name UK organisations already working on your issue
items.exercise: Write three sentences, one per horizon, each starting with a role title and ending with a measurable result. Add a fallback for the riskiest one.

items.title: Complete Chevening Essay Example (Networking answer)
items.author: Mirza Idham Saifuddin

criteria.how: Draws on a national scholars' alumni network of about 10,000, a corporate scholarship, a young entrepreneurs' association and a rural education non-profit.
A funder relationship led to a supervisory offer; networks gave him a regional speaking slot.

structure.what: His work forced him to build networks.
Four named networks, each with what it gave him.
Wants to collaborate with Chevening alumni on global issues.

techniques: Named organisations and an alumni count
Covers corporate, government and NGO networks to show range
weaknesses: Reads as a list of memberships; no single relationship is developed in depth
Results of the networks are thin
borrow: Show range: one corporate, one public, one community network
Quantify the size of a network you can mobilise
Then go deep on one relationship (fix his weakness)
items.exercise: Map your networks in a 3-column table (sector, name, what it produced). Then write 150 words about the single most productive one.

items.title: Complete Chevening Essay Example (Studying in the UK answer)
items.author: Mirza Idham Saifuddin

criteria.how: Three entrepreneurship master's options (Leeds, Warwick, Nottingham), each with one angle: enterprise award/alumni, decision-making, technology.
Says any of them would help him build enterprise in his rural hometown.

structure.what: Passion for running businesses.
One feature per university.
Impact on hometown entrepreneurship.

techniques: Uses an alumni count to show an ecosystem
weaknesses: Very short; leaves words unused
General UK statistics add little; no modules named
borrow: Use every word allowed; add a module per course
Replace national statistics with course-specific evidence
State what you will do in the first year back
items.exercise: Rewrite your why-UK paragraph replacing every general claim about the UK with one fact specific to your course.

items.title: Victory Ojating's Chevening story
items.author: Victory Ojating
items.quote: wove the four essays together into a cohesive narrative

criteria.c: All four criteria as one story
criteria.how: Describes treating leadership, networking, course and career answers as chapters of one narrative built on her food and nutrition career at a multinational and roles with global food-system youth networks.
Says she used verifiable numbers and a Situation-Task-Action-Result-Lesson pattern.

structure.what: Drafted months before the window opened.
Chose universities partly on language-test exemptions and emailed potential academics.
Same mission thread runs through all four essays.
Friends and mentors critiqued drafts.

weaknesses: Essay text not public, so the reader cannot see the execution
Advice partly generic (believe in yourself)
borrow: Write a one-sentence mission and check every essay against it
Add an 'L' (lesson) line to each STAR example
Draft before the portal opens
items.exercise: Write your one-sentence mission. Then list one example per Chevening essay and one line saying how each proves that mission.

items.title: The Novice Guide to Becoming a Chevening Scholar
items.author: Abraham Ologundudu

criteria.how: Built his networking answer around one sustained professional relationship, showing benefits flowing both ways over time, then linked it to the Chevening community.
Used three connected milestones from his own ventures (a journal, a conference, a digital agency) with dates and statistics.

structure.what: One relationship rather than many contacts.
What each side gained.
Shows it lasted.
How the habit transfers to UK/alumni relationships.

techniques: Explicit link to Chevening's goal of lasting UK ties
Bridges an unusual degree switch (physics/education to media for development)
weaknesses: No essay text, so tone and evidence can't be judged
Advice on course essay is general
borrow: Build the networking essay on one relationship, told over time
State what the other person gained
Close with how you'll keep UK relationships alive
items.exercise: Choose one person you have worked with for over a year. Write 150 words: how you met, what each of you gained, and what you built together.

items.title: Tips on Applying for Commonwealth Shared Scholarship 2020
items.author: Runcie C.W. Chidebe
items.quote: Nigeria has the world's second-highest number of deaths in children under five

criteria.how: Opened with sourced national health statistics (child mortality, HIV, cancer cases and deaths) and linked them to his work in cancer control.

Committed to apply skills through the cancer non-profit he leads and through volunteering with the health ministry and parliamentary committees, with year-by-year milestones and named beneficiary groups.

structure.what: Global, national, local burden with citations.
Where he will use new skills (named organisation and public bodies).
Primary and secondary impact areas, beneficiaries, dated milestones.
Growth tracking, reporting, statistics.

techniques: Named beneficiary groups (patients, volunteers, co-infected people, older people)
weaknesses: Measurement plan is broad; no baseline or target numbers given
No course modules named in the university section
borrow: Cite two national statistics with source and year
List beneficiaries by group, not 'Nigerians'
Give each milestone a year
items.exercise: Write your impact chain in four lines: problem statistic (with source) → what you will do → who benefits (named group) → how you will measure it by a given year.

items.title: Winning Fulbright Fellowship Sample Essay: Personal Statement 2018
items.author: Patrick M. Szot
items.quote: My past is evidence that teaching can absolutely change lives.

criteria.how: Shows resilience (working from 18 after family financial collapse) and international growth via a study-abroad scholarship.
Uses his Polish heritage as a bridge to support Polish students.

structure.what: Baking family cookies.
Recession, divorce, money trouble.
Work and a scholarship abroad.
A teacher who widened his view.
Teach and develop student leaders in Poland, tied to his business goals.

techniques: Warm sensory opening followed by contrast
Named mentor gives credit and credibility
weaknesses: Hardship section takes space that could show teaching evidence
Link between consulting goals and teaching is loose
borrow: Open with a small sensory memory, then the turn
Credit a named mentor
Say how your identity helps you serve the host community
items.exercise: Write a 70-word opening built on one smell, sound or object from home, then one sentence where things changed.

items.title: Sample personal essay that won me the Fulbright in 2003
items.author: Marc Maxmeister

criteria.how: Peace Corps teaching in The Gambia, then computer-literacy projects across four schools and national IT workshops.
Proposes a follow-up survey of IT in West African schools to measure progress.

structure.what: Rejects the 'saving the world' story.
International childhood.
Seeing extreme poverty changed his career plan.
Living in the community, learning leadership.
From science teaching to IT training.
Science teaching should build problem solving.
Survey to measure change.

techniques: Opens by refusing a cliché, which earns trust
Projects scale up step by step
weaknesses: Long; could cut background
Some outsider framing of poverty could be told more from local partners' view
borrow: Name the cliché you will not use, then tell the real story
Show a belief you changed
Finish with a measurable project
items.exercise: Write one sentence naming the cliché people expect from your story, then 100 words on what really happened.

items.title: Motivation Letter of Stipendium Hungaricum
items.author: Aswarini Puspa Arnas

criteria.how: Maths education graduate seeking a mathematics master's to become a lecturer-researcher.
Cites Hungary's mathematical tradition and named Hungarian mathematicians, plus safety and old universities.
States she will return to her home university as a lecturer.

structure.what: Famous line about maths as language of the universe.
Degree with honours.
Lecturer and researcher.
Tutoring.
Culture and mathematicians.
Home university and ranked choices.
Courteous close.

techniques: Names discipline-specific Hungarian figures, which shows homework
weaknesses: Opening with a famous quote is common
Long praise of Hungary; little on specific courses or research interests
borrow: Name two people from the host country in your field
State the job and institution you return to
Spend more words on the programme than on the country
items.exercise: Find two researchers or inventors from the host country in your field. Write 80 words linking their work to what you want to study.

items.title: Stipendium Hungaricum Sample Motivation Letter
items.author: glyzz (The Scholar's Odyssey)
items.quote: A snowflake that will vanish in the dawn of spring

criteria.how: First in family at college, hardship, and proving doubters wrong.
Interest shifted to sustainable development and nuclear energy, noting research is undervalued at home.
Admits study-abroad challenges and points to resilience.

structure.what: First-generation student; scholarship as chance for self and nation.
Personal hardship and others' low expectations.
Change of interest to energy and sustainability.
Resilience abroad.
Not exceptional, but determined.

weaknesses: Heavy on hardship, light on academic evidence
No named Hungarian programme features
borrow: Name a gap in your country's research system you'll help fill
Admit one challenge and show your plan for it
Use one strong image, once
items.exercise: Write 100 words: one obstacle you faced, one concrete step you took, and the academic result.

items.title: Sample MEXT Field of Study and Research Program Plan with Analysis
items.author: James Chabin (published by MEXT scholar Travis Senzaki with commentary)

criteria.how: Clear comparative question (Japanese vs US aid approaches in Mexico's auto workforce) with document analysis plus phone surveys.
Specific region where he has NGO contacts, language skills and a four-semester timeline.
Undergraduate thesis that first introduced him to Japanese development theory.

structure.what: Degree, thesis and current think-tank job.
Research title and gap.
Sources from three agencies plus mobile surveys.
Semester-by-semester plan.
Target journals and policy relevance.

techniques: Gap tied to Japan's own interests
weaknesses: Analysis method for 'identifying theories' is thin (noted by the publisher)
Survey sample and questions not specified; naming one university can hurt other placements
borrow: Explain why Japan specifically benefits from your topic
Show you can access your data (contacts, language)
Give a per-semester plan
items.exercise: Write your research question in one sentence, then three bullet points: data source, how you get access, how you will analyse it.

items.award: Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program (University of Edinburgh)
items.title: How to answer your Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program essays (with real essay example)
items.author: Mirabelle Morah

criteria.how: Course representative for 100+ students and media officer for a university social-enterprise team.
A project turning discarded billboard banners into water-resistant school bags for low-income pupils, employing a local artisan.

structure.what: A novel read at 13 sparked her belief in storytelling for change.
Student representative role with a number.
Upcycling project with beneficiaries and a local job.
Shows she understands circular economy ideas.

techniques: Origin story from a named African novel
Fits a lot into a short limit
Named beneficiaries and a local hire
weaknesses: Only partial text, so no view of barriers section
Few outcome numbers for the bag project
borrow: Name the book, person or moment that started your interest
Describe one small project with who it helped
Link it to one concept from your field
items.exercise: In 120 words describe a small project you ran: material/resource, who benefited, how many, and the idea from your field it shows.

items.title: How to Win the Gates Cambridge Scholarship
items.author: Madeleine Ary Hahne
items.quote: Show how the lessons learned there can apply more broadly to the human race

criteria.how: Framed her research on religious responses to climate change as key to collective climate action.
Justified the topic by arguing a small denial group holds outsized political and cultural power, so it must be studied.

structure.what: Faith communities and climate change.
Small group, big influence.
Shows she is suited to study it.
Generalises beyond the case.

techniques: A counter-intuitive statistic to justify a niche topic
Scales a local case to a global issue
weaknesses: Statement not shared
Advice is US-centred
borrow: Use one surprising number to show why a niche matters
End with how your findings help people beyond your case
Contact the supervisor before writing
items.exercise: Write two sentences: 'Most people think X. But [number] shows Y, which is why my research on Z matters.'

items.title: My Rhodes Scholarship Application Journey
items.author: Daniel Mutia Mwendwa
items.quote: less about the activity you were involved in

criteria.how: Volunteering, community projects and co-founding a venture that trains young tech innovators in Kenya and Rwanda.
Showed curiosity and academic interests as an engineering student and Mastercard Foundation Scholar.
Chose reflection on impact over listing activities.

structure.what: Journey from home to university.
Service, enterprise, study.
What each experience meant.
Hopes for Kenya, Africa, the world.

techniques: Wrote freely first to find his own voice
weaknesses: Statement not published
Little detail on Oxford course fit in the post
borrow: Free-write a first draft with no rules, then edit
For each activity, write one line on what it changed
Use a past-present-future spine
items.exercise: Pick your top activity. Write 3 lines: what you did, what changed for others, what it changed in you.

items.title: Applying to the Schwarzman Scholars Program
items.author: Cristina Pogorevici

criteria.how: Leadership essay on a student council overseeing 40+ clubs, where she built a central application system for club recruitment under resource limits.
Statement of purpose about understanding Western and Eastern schools of thought.

structure.what: Organisation and scale.
Fragmented recruitment, limited resources.
Designed a central system.
Constraints drove innovation.

techniques: Systems-level fix rather than one event
weaknesses: Essays not shared
Statement theme is broad; needs a concrete China link
borrow: Choose a leadership story where you fixed a system
Give the scale in numbers
Test every paragraph against 'Why this programme?'
items.exercise: Describe a process you redesigned (150 words): what was broken, what you built, how many people it affected.

items.title: Winning a scholarship in France is possible: Eiffel Excellence Scholarship
items.author: Juan (Vive la Francia)
items.quote: consistency between my academic career and my professional project

criteria.how: Highlighted his thesis on corporate social responsibility and a recognised conference presentation.
Argued that European best practice learned in France would support his home country's development.

structure.what: CSR and governance.
Thesis and conference.
Management skills from an MBA.
International exposure and value for home country.

techniques: Consistency between past research and future plan
weaknesses: Year and full text not given
Generic 'global exposure' argument
borrow: Draw a straight line from your thesis to your next degree
Mention one recognition of your work
Name one French practice you want to bring home
items.exercise: Write 3 sentences: my thesis/project was on X; the next degree adds Y; at home I will use it to do Z.

items.title: On Winning an Erasmus Mundus Scholarship. Part 2: Capitalizing on Unfair Advantages
items.author: Nene Abayateye

criteria.how: Profile built on an energy-sector job (2.5 years), a thesis on concentrated solar power and relevant coursework.
Three European languages at stated levels, conferences abroad and professional membership.

structure.what: Eleven profile elements, from academics to hobbies.
Turns each into an 'unfair advantage' for the consortium.

techniques: Language levels stated precisely (C1, B2, A2)
weaknesses: Profile breakdown, not the letter itself
Some elements (typing speed) add little
borrow: Audit your profile for 3 assets peers rarely have
State language levels with CEFR grades
Match your thesis to a programme track
items.exercise: List 10 things in your profile. Circle the 3 rarest among applicants and write one sentence on how each helps the programme.

items.award: Swedish Institute Scholarships for Global Professionals
items.title: My 4 biggest lessons-learned when applying for the SISGP
items.author: Nguyen (Study in Sweden blogger)

criteria.how: Says the letter must link personal values and achievements to the scholarship's aims and wider social impact.
Kept CV, motivation letter and experience forms telling the same story.

structure.what: State what you care about.
Go beyond the CV with reflection.
Connect to SI goals and home-country impact.

weaknesses: No letter excerpts
Advice general
borrow: Read your CV and letter side by side and remove contradictions
Add the 'why' behind each CV item
End with your home-country contribution
items.exercise: Take your top 3 CV lines and write one sentence each explaining why it mattered to you and to others.

items.title: A Journey to KGSP/GKS: Personal Statement
items.author: bonaintan

criteria.how: Found her angle by answering 'Why Korea?' and 'Why me?' before writing.
Opened with a family background story, as the GKS form asks for family, education and experiences.

structure.what: Family story.
Family, education, experiences, motivation for Korea.
Lessons from each experience.

techniques: Three months of drafting and outside proofreading
weaknesses: Statement not public; year/university not stated
Advice could apply to any scholarship
borrow: Write your answers to 'Why Korea?' and 'Why me?' first
Order paragraphs as the prompt lists them
Close each experience with a lesson
items.exercise: Answer 'Why Korea?' and 'Why me?' in 40 words each. Then turn each into a paragraph opener.

items.title: PTDF Overseas Scholarship Scheme: My Personal Experience (II)

criteria.how: Made sure the proposal tied directly to the Nigerian oil and gas industry.

Owned his own story, not a generic hardship one.
Quantified past work.
Industry link stated plainly.

Author name not given in post

Use one number per paragraph
Only claim what you can defend at interview
